title: Rivera Lab Meeting: Enhancer Activity Model and MPRA Validation Design
description: Synthetic computational-biology lab meeting for testing Chumi. Part 1: Maya presents a convolution plus attention model that predicts enhancer activity (ATAC-seq accessibility) from DNA sequence in erythroid progenitors. Part 2: design and statistics for a lentiMPRA validation screen. Wei code-switches between Mandarin and English technical terms.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: OK, let's get started. I think everyone's here. Quick housekeeping first: the cluster maintenance got moved, so the GPU queue might be slow this week. Plan around that. OK. Maya, you're presenting today, so whenever you're ready.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Thanks. So I want to give an update on the enhancer model, and then we agreed to use the second half to plan the validation experiment. Let me share my screen. Can everyone see the title slide?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Yep, it's up.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Great. Quick recap, mostly for Sam, since this is your first lab meeting with us. The goal of the project is to predict enhancer activity directly from DNA sequence in one hematopoietic cell type. We're working in erythroid progenitors, because that's where we have the deepest chromatin data. And the long-term plan is to take the most interesting predictions and test them in a lenti MPRA screen.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Before you go on, remind everyone what the training label is. When you say enhancer activity, what does the model actually see?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. The labels come from ATAC seq. We call peaks in the erythroid cells, and each training example is a one thousand base pair window centered on a peak, along with matched background windows as negatives. The model predicts the accessibility signal at the center of the window. So strictly speaking, it predicts accessibility, and we're using accessibility as a proxy for enhancer activity.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: I want to flag that right now, because it's going to come back later. Accessible is not the same thing as active. Plenty of open chromatin doesn't drive any expression at all.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Agreed. That's exactly why the MPRA matters. If the predictions don't hold up in the MPRA, then we've learned something important about the label.

lines.speaker: Wei
lines.text: 对，accessibility 和 activity 真的不一样。我们之前在另外一个 cell line 里面也看到过，很多很强的 ATAC peak，在 MPRA 里面基本上没有 signal。

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yeah, I remember that. OK, so the architecture. The front end is a stack of convolutional layers. The first layer has three hundred filters of width nineteen, and those tend to learn motif-like patterns. Then there are dilated convolutions to grow the receptive field, and then four attention layers on top, so the model can learn interactions between motifs that are far apart in the window.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Why both, though? Couldn't the attention layers learn the motifs by themselves?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: In principle, yes. But in practice the convolutions are a really good inductive bias for short motifs, and they shrink the sequence length before the attention layers, which saves a lot of memory. Full attention over a thousand individual base pairs gets expensive quickly.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: How are you picking the negatives? Because if they're just random background, the model can get a long way by learning GC content, and that tells us nothing about enhancers.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: They're GC-matched. For every peak, I sample a background window from the same chromosome with GC content within one percent. I also train with reverse complement augmentation, so the model sees both strands, and at prediction time I average the forward and reverse complement predictions.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Good. And what about peaks near promoters? Those are going to be the easiest to predict, and they're not enhancers.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: I removed anything within two kilobases of an annotated transcription start site. That took out about eighteen percent of the peaks.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Did you try it without attention? Because if the convolution-only model does just as well, I'd rather have the simpler model.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: I did, that's the next slide. The convolution-only baseline gets a Pearson correlation of about zero point six two on held-out peaks. With attention, it's zero point six eight. So it's a real gain, but it's not, um,

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Six points. Sorry to cut you off. Is that a single run?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: No, that's the average over five random seeds. The standard deviation across seeds is about zero point zero one, so the gap is well outside the seed noise.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: OK, good. Keep going.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So the full training set is about one hundred twenty thousand sequences. One thing I looked at this week is how performance scales with the amount of training data. As you can see in this plot, the curve flattens after about fifty thousand training sequences. Past that point, adding more data barely moves the validation correlation.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Sorry, which line is the attention model?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The blue one. Orange is the convolution-only baseline. They both plateau, but the blue one plateaus higher, and the gap stays about the same the whole way across.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: That plateau worries me a bit. It could mean you've extracted everything the sequence can tell you, or it could mean you're limited by noise in the labels. Those have very different implications for what we do next.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: I think it's label noise, at least partly. The ATAC replicates only correlate with each other at about zero point eight, so that's roughly a ceiling for any model.

lines.speaker: Wei
lines.text: 这个 ceiling 很重要。如果 replicate 之间的 correlation 只有零点八，那 model 能到零点六八其实已经不错了。你可以算一个 noise ceiling，直接画在这个 plot 上面。

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Sorry, how do you actually compute a noise ceiling?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Roughly, you ask how well one replicate predicts another replicate. The model can't predict the measurement noise, so that's about the best you could ever hope for.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Yes, please add that to the plot. Any reviewer is going to ask about it.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Will do. OK, so the validation setup. Right now I'm holding out ten percent of the peaks for validation and another ten percent for test, sampled randomly across the genome.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Randomly across peaks, or randomly across chromosomes?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Across peaks. So peaks from the same chromosome can end up in both training and test.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Hmm. OK. I have some thoughts about that, but let's hold them for the second half. Show us the attribution results first.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Sure. So to understand what the model is actually using, I computed attribution maps with integrated gradients, and I also ran in silico mutagenesis, where you mutate every position to each of the other three bases and measure how much the prediction changes. The two methods mostly agree, which is reassuring.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: How long does the mutagenesis take? That sounds like a lot of forward passes.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's three thousand forward passes per sequence, so I only ran it on the top two thousand predicted enhancers. It took most of a night on one GPU.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: And for integrated gradients, what did you use as the reference sequence? That choice changes the maps quite a lot.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: I used ten dinucleotide-shuffled versions of each sequence and averaged over them. I tried an all-zeros reference too, and the maps were noisier, but the main motifs were the same.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Fine. So what did you find?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So this is the part I really want feedback on. When I cluster the attribution patterns, there's a subset of enhancers, roughly fifteen percent of the top two thousand, where the model seems to rely heavily on a GATA motif. The high-attribution bases line up with the GATA consensus, and when you mutate that motif in silico, the predicted accessibility drops sharply.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Before anyone gets excited, how consistent is that across replicates?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's the big caveat. The GATA pattern only shows up in models trained on two of the three replicates. When I train on the third replicate, the GATA cluster basically disappears. So it might be a batch effect. Replicates one and two were sequenced together, and replicate three was a separate run, a few months later. So I wouldn't claim this yet.

lines.speaker: Wei
lines.text: 我觉得这个 GATA motif 的结果可能是真的，因为在 erythroid cells 里面 GATA1 本来就很重要，它基本上就是 master regulator。如果 model 完全没有学到 GATA，我反而会觉得奇怪。但是我们需要看第三个 replicate 为什么不一样。

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: I hear you, Wei, and I agree GATA1 is exactly what we'd expect biologically. But that's what makes me nervous. When a result matches our expectations, we stop checking it. Two out of three replicates, and the two that agree were sequenced in the same batch? Until we've checked the third replicate, my working assumption is that this is a batch artifact.

lines.speaker: Wei
lines.text: 但是 batch effect 一般影响的是比较 global 的东西，比如 GC content 或者 fragment length。它不太会刚好产生一个这么 specific 的 GATA motif。

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Not necessarily. Suppose the third run had lower library complexity. Then the weaker peaks drop out, and if the GATA enhancers happen to be the weaker peaks, you'd see exactly this pattern. I'm not saying it isn't real. I'm saying we don't know yet.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's roughly where I am too. I think it's plausible, but I don't want it on a poster until I understand what's going on with replicate three.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Do we have any GATA1 binding data in these cells? CUT and Tag, anything? That would be an independent line of evidence.

lines.speaker: Wei
lines.text: 我们有一个 GATA1 的 CUT and Tag，是去年做的，但是只有一个 replicate，quality 也一般，所以最多只能当作 supporting evidence。

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Then it's suggestive at best. OK, so for the record: the GATA result is interesting, it is not confirmed, and it doesn't go on any slides outside this room until the third replicate is sorted out.

lines.speaker: Wei
lines.text: 好，我同意先不下结论。不过我还是 bet 它是真的。

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Noted. We'll see who's right.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Can I ask about the attention layers? Did you look at the attention weights directly? Like, do any of the heads connect the GATA sites to other motifs?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: I looked, but attention weights are notoriously hard to interpret, so I wouldn't read much into them. There's one head that seems to link GATA sites to nearby E box motifs, which would fit with GATA1 working together with its usual partner factors. But honestly, I'd call that anecdotal.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Agreed. Let's not go down that road today. Anything else on the model before we move on?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Just one more slide. I compared the model to a simple baseline that only counts known motifs in each window. The motif count baseline gets a correlation of about zero point four five, so the deep model is clearly capturing more than motif presence. My guess is that spacing and orientation matter, but I haven't tested that directly.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: That's a nice comparison. Keep it in. It answers the question of whether we need deep learning at all, which someone always asks.

lines.speaker: Wei
lines.text: 还有一个小建议，motif count 的 baseline 太简单了。你可以再加一个 gapped k-mer 的 model，这样比较会更 fair 一点。

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Good idea. I'll add that if I have time.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Great. OK, let's switch gears and talk about the validation experiment and the statistics for the new screen. Maya, do you want to keep driving?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Sure, I'll start, and Wei can jump in on the cloning side. So the plan is a lenti MPRA in the same erythroid progenitors. I'm proposing about ten thousand sequences in total. Roughly six thousand would be predicted enhancers chosen across the full range of model scores, not just the top ones, so we can actually check calibration. Then about three thousand variant sequences, where we disrupt the highest-attribution motif in a top enhancer, including the GATA ones. And then about a thousand controls.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: What kind of controls?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Five hundred scrambled sequences with matched GC content as negatives, and five hundred known strong enhancers from published screens as positives.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Good. And I like that the variants include the GATA enhancers. That's a much cleaner test of the GATA story than anything we can do computationally. If disrupting the GATA motif kills activity in the MPRA, that's real evidence.

lines.speaker: Wei
lines.text: 对，这个 design 我觉得很好。不过 library size 要注意一下。一万个 sequence，如果每个 sequence 要两百个 barcode，那就是两百万个 barcode，transduction 的时候需要非常多的 cells，coverage 才够。

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Sorry, how do the barcodes get assigned? Are they part of the synthesized oligo?

lines.speaker: Wei
lines.text: 不是，barcode 是 random 的，是 cloning 的时候用 PCR 加上去的。然后我们要先做一轮 sequencing，把每个 barcode 和它对应的 sequence 配对起来，这一步叫 association。

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Right, and that's why barcodes per variant is a real design decision and not just a free parameter. More barcodes gives you a better estimate of each sequence's activity, but every barcode has to be represented in enough cells, and these progenitors don't transduce nearly as well as the usual cell lines.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So that's the tradeoff I want to settle. With one hundred barcodes per variant, my simulations say we can detect a two-fold change in activity with about eighty percent power. With two hundred, we get closer to ninety-five percent power, but we'd need roughly twice as many cells and twice the sequencing depth.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: And how many replicates are you assuming in those simulations?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Three biological replicates, meaning three independent transductions on different days.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Three is the minimum I'd accept. Honestly, I'd prefer four, but I understand the cell numbers are the bottleneck. Let's say three, and we'll revisit if the first replicate looks noisy.

lines.speaker: Wei
lines.text: 三个 replicate 应该没问题。我们上次在别的 cell type 里面做的时候，三个 replicate 之间的 correlation 已经很高了。

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: OK, so three replicates. Then the statistics. For each barcode we get a DNA count and an RNA count, and activity is basically the log ratio of RNA over DNA, aggregated over all the barcodes for each sequence.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: What happens to barcodes with very low DNA counts? The ratio gets unstable when the denominator is tiny.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: I'll drop barcodes with fewer than ten DNA reads, and require at least ten passing barcodes per sequence. Anything below that gets reported as missing, not as inactive.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Good. And report how many sequences get dropped that way, in every replicate. Now, what do the counts themselves look like, distribution-wise?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Very overdispersed. I looked at pilot data from Wei's earlier screen, and for barcodes with the same expected count, the variance is something like five to ten times the mean. So a Poisson model is clearly wrong. I'm planning to use a negative binomial model, where each sequence's activity is a coefficient and the DNA counts go in as an offset.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Sorry, this might be a really basic question, but why is it called negative binomial? What's negative about it?

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Ha, that's a fair question, and honestly the name is a bit of a historical accident. One way to define it is the number of failures you see before you reach a fixed number of successes, and the name comes from a binomial expansion with a negative exponent. But for our purposes, just think of it as a Poisson distribution with one extra parameter that lets the variance be bigger than the mean.

lines.speaker: Wei
lines.text: 我第一次学的时候也有一样的问题。其实你可以把它理解成很多个 Poisson 混在一起，每个 Poisson 的 rate 都不一样，也就是 gamma Poisson mixture。

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Oh, OK. So is that related to the beta binomial thing people use for allele counts?

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Related in spirit, but not the same, and that is definitely a tangent for another day. Let's get back to the design.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: OK. So with ten thousand sequences we're doing ten thousand tests, which means we need multiple testing correction. The plan is to control the false discovery rate at five percent. And for the variants, the test is whether each variant differs from its matched reference sequence, so that's a separate family of about three thousand tests.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Make sure you define those families before you see the data. If you pool everything into one FDR correction after the fact, you'll be tempted to slice it whichever way gives the most hits.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yes, that's fair. The families should be fixed up front.

lines.speaker: Wei
lines.text: 还有，FDR 最好用 scrambled 的 negative control 来 calibrate 一下 null distribution。如果 negative control 的 p value 不是 uniform 的，那就说明 model 有问题。

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's a great point. The scrambled controls basically give us an empirical null for free.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: OK. Now let me come back to the thing I flagged earlier, the held-out split. I think the random split is a real problem. Neighboring peaks are often correlated, some enhancers overlap each other, and there are repeats and duplicated regions all over the genome. If nearly identical sequences end up in both training and test, your test correlation is inflated. That's leakage.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: I was worried about that too. How big do you think the effect is?

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: In my experience it can be a few points of correlation, sometimes more. Which, notice, is about the same size as the gain you're getting from the attention layers. So it matters.

lines.speaker: Wei
lines.text: 对，标准的做法是按 chromosome 来分。比如说 chromosome 八和九做 test，chromosome 十做 validation，其他的全部用来 train。这样 sequence 之间就不会 leak。

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Exactly. And there's a second reason, which connects to the screen. If we pick the MPRA candidates from chromosomes the model never saw during training, then the MPRA becomes a genuinely out-of-sample test of the model. Otherwise we're partly testing sequences it has already memorized.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That makes sense. So the MPRA library should be drawn mostly from the held-out chromosomes.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Mostly, yes. Maya, can you rerun the model with the chromosome-level holdout split? No rush, whenever you get to it.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Sure, I can do that. Should I redo the attribution analysis on the new split too, or just the performance numbers?

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Start with the performance numbers and the scaling curve. If the attention advantage survives the new split, then redo the attribution.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Would it also make sense to hold out by cell type? Like, train on erythroid cells and test on megakaryocytes or something?

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: That's a different question, generalization across cell types. It's interesting, but it's out of scope for this project. Let's keep it to one cell type for now.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: OK. So going back to the library, the next thing we need is the actual barcode design. Wei, you've done this before. What do you need from me?

lines.speaker: Wei
lines.text: 我需要你的 final sequence list，还有每个 sequence 的 category，就是 enhancer、variant 还是 control。然后 barcode 和 primer 的 design 我来做。

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The list is already on the lab drive, in the MPRA folder.

lines.speaker: Wei
lines.text: 好，那没问题。barcode design 的 spreadsheet 我这个星期五之前发给大家，by Friday。里面会列出不同 barcode 数量需要的 cell number 和 sequencing depth。

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Perfect. So Wei sends the barcode design spreadsheet by Friday. That's the one hard deadline we have, because the oligo order depends on it.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And that spreadsheet is what we'll use to decide on the barcodes, right? One hundred versus two hundred per variant?

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: It'll inform it, but I don't think the spreadsheet alone answers it. Part of it is a judgment call about how small an effect we actually care about.

lines.speaker: Wei
lines.text: 我个人倾向用两百个 barcode。很多 variant 的 effect 其实很小，如果 power 不够，最后大部分 variant 都是 not significant，结果很难解释。

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: But with two hundred, we might not be able to get enough cells for three replicates. I'd rather have three solid replicates at one hundred barcodes than two shaky ones at two hundred.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Both fair points. I don't think we're going to settle one hundred versus two hundred barcodes today. Let's leave that open.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Could we run a small pilot with both and see which one gives cleaner data?

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Maybe. That costs time, though, so let's not decide that today either. Everyone think about it.

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: OK, we're about out of time. Wei, Friday for the spreadsheet, right?

lines.speaker: Wei
lines.text: 对，Friday。没问题。

lines.speaker: PI
lines.text: Great. And the barcode number is still an open question, so think about whether one hundred or two hundred barcodes per variant makes more sense, and we'll come back to it. Thanks, Maya, really nice progress. And Sam, welcome again.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Thanks, everyone.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Thanks, Professor Rivera. See you all next week.
